entries_new.name: MoonDAO
entries_new.mechanism: Coordinates members and money online through a DAO, with a stated aim of a settlement on the Moon.
entries_new.story: MoonDAO is an online group organised as a DAO, a decentralized autonomous organization, meaning members vote through software instead of working under a company board. The Network State Atlas, a directory of such projects, lists it as a global virtual community active since 2021 with more than 5,000 members. It funds and takes part in challenges meant to advance human presence in space and move toward a lunar settlement. The listing names no physical base and gives no funding total.

entries_new.name: Logos
entries_new.mechanism: Builds its own communication and governance software so a community can run itself without a host state's systems.
entries_new.story: Logos is an online project listed by the Network State Atlas, a directory of network-state projects, as a global virtual community active since 2022 with more than 10,000 community members. A network state is an online community that hopes to gain land and recognition later. Logos describes its aim as a self-sovereign, privacy-preserving, decentralized network state, and it builds communication tools and governance systems for that purpose. The listing names no founders and no physical site.

entries_new.name: Nation3
entries_new.passports: NFT passports issued by the project
entries_new.mechanism: Issues blockchain passports and offers its own online jurisdiction and governance to people who sign up.
entries_new.story: Nation3 is an online project that describes itself as a web3 solarpunk society and a digital-first sovereign cloud nation, meaning a country meant to exist mainly on the internet. The Network State Atlas lists it as active since 2022, with its own jurisdiction, governance system and passports issued as NFTs, which are tokens recorded on a blockchain. The same directory counts more than 5,000 passport holders. No state is reported as accepting these passports, and the listing gives no physical territory.

entries_new.name: VitaDAO
entries_new.mechanism: Pools money from token holders and decides by online vote which longevity research to fund.
entries_new.story: VitaDAO is an online group that funds early-stage research into longevity, the science of extending healthy life. It is organised as a DAO, a decentralized autonomous organization in which token holders vote on decisions. The Network State Atlas lists it as a virtual global community active since 2021, with more than 10,000 token holders and over $2.5 million invested in longevity projects. It is included in network-state directories as a community with its own purpose and funds, and the listing names no land or physical base.

entries_new.name: Closer
entries_new.mechanism: Provides coordination software for intentional communities in place of a shared government.
entries_new.story: Closer is a technology project listed by the Network State Atlas as a global virtual community active since 2020, with more than 1,000 users. It builds software for regenerative living, meaning communities that aim to restore the land they live on. The platform helps communities coordinate, share resources and develop models for living together. The directory names no founders. Closer itself holds no territory in the listing; it supplies tools that other communities use.

entries_new.name: RadicalxChange
entries_new.mechanism: Develops and tests alternative voting and property rules that communities can adopt.
entries_new.story: RadicalxChange is a movement that works on new methods for voting, property rights and collective decisions. The Network State Atlas says it was founded on ideas from the book Radical Markets, lists it as a global virtual community active since 2018, and counts more than 10,000 community members. Its work takes the form of research and experiments, with the stated aim of reimagining the building blocks of democracy and markets. It claims no territory, and the listing names no founders.

entries_new.name: Don't Die
entries_new.founder: Bryan Johnson (associated with the movement in the directory)
entries_new.mechanism: Gathers followers online around one founding goal, as network-state theory proposes, without any land.
entries_new.story: Don't Die is a movement led by Bryan Johnson, the Network State Atlas says, aimed at reversing aging and extending life through health routines and protocols. The directory classes it as a network state, an online community organised around one shared goal, based in the USA and active worldwide since 2023, with more than 100,000 followers. Its stated aim is to end the causes of human and planetary death. It holds no territory of its own in the listing.

entries_new.name: Cohere
entries_new.mechanism: Connects shared houses in several countries through one membership.
entries_new.story: Cohere is a network of coliving communities, places where members share housing and workspace, across the Americas. The Network State Atlas lists it as active since 2022 with more than 500 members and gives its locations as Antigua, Ecuador, Brazil and Global, a list that does not name a single town. The P2P Foundation's copy of the Network State Dashboard describes the spaces as member-owned. The listing reports no claim to independence.

entries_new.name: Kift
entries_new.mechanism: Offers members shared land and services at scattered sites instead of one territory.
entries_new.story: Kift builds a community for people who live in vans. The Network State Atlas lists it as active since 2021, with more than 5,000 members, and says it gives vanlifers and nomads access to land, resources and company at multiple sites across North America, listed as the USA, Canada and Global. The directory names no single site or founder. It appears in the Network State Dashboard list under the description of building a vanlife community, and no claim of independence is reported.

entries_new.name: Proof of Humanity
entries_new.laws: Disputes go to Kleros or a compatible system
entries_new.mechanism: Replaces a government identity register with a list of people vouched for by members, with disputes decided by an online court.
entries_new.story: Proof of Humanity is an identity list for people on the Ethereum blockchain, described in 2021 by Kleros, the online court project that handles its disputes. To join, a person uploads a video of themselves and pays a deposit, and a registered member vouches for them. Anyone can challenge an entry as a duplicate, a deceased person or someone who does not exist, by posting a deposit, and the dispute goes to Kleros. Registered profiles expire after a year and receive UBI tokens, a form of basic income paid in cryptocurrency. The Network State Dashboard list calls this building decentralized democracy.

sources.t: Proof of Humanity: an explainer (Kleros blog)

entries_new.name: build_republic
entries_new.founder: Angelo (first name only in the source)
entries_new.mechanism: Offers software for running a startup city as a shared protocol.
entries_new.story: build_republic is a software project listed on the Network State Dashboard as building a protocol for startup cities, which are new cities planned as ventures. A newsletter on network states dated 7 October 2022 reported that its public beta launched that week and said its infrastructure seemed a building block toward what the investor Balaji Srinivasan describes as a network state dashboard. The newsletter names the founder only as Angelo and gives no location or user figures. The sources do not say whether it is still running.

sources.t: The State of Network States in Fall (Future of Living)

entries_new.name: Jur
entries_new.cost: $1 million seed investment from Tim Draper
entries_new.mechanism: Sells private arbitration online so parties can settle disputes outside national courts.
entries_new.story: Jur is a company founded in Switzerland that the Network State Dashboard list describes as creating an efficient jurisdiction for the digital economy. Its founder and chief executive is Alessandro Palombo. It launched an online dispute service, the Open Justice Platform, in beta on 31 March 2021, for civil and commercial claims between $5,000 and $1.5 million, and said it would meet UNCITRAL requirements, the United Nations trade law standards. The investor Tim Draper put in $1 million. It planned to add a token that arbitrators would stake against corruption.
entries_new.anchor: Switzerland (country of founding; no town given)

sources.t: Tim Draper invests $1M in blockchain-based dispute resolution platform (LawSites)

entries_new.name: Noma Collective
entries_new.mechanism: Moves members between temporary sites arranged for them, with no permanent settlement.
entries_new.story: Noma Collective calls itself a network society for digital nomads and remote builders, people who work online while moving between countries. The Network School dashboard, a published list of such projects, says it was founded in 2021, first ran trips in Placencia, Belize, and acquired the travel group Hacker Paradise in 2024. It runs popups of three to four weeks in which members get workspace, housing and events arranged for them. The page gives no member count or founder and reports no territorial claim.
entries_new.anchor: First trips at Placencia, Belize; no permanent site

entries_new.name: The Mu
entries_new.mechanism: Holds temporary villages in different host countries rather than holding territory.
entries_new.story: The Mu organises popup villages, temporary gatherings where people live and work together for a few weeks. The Network School dashboard says it was founded in 2023, has hosted five popups and calls itself one of the longest-running organisers of such villages. Events named on the page took place in Chiang Mai, Thailand, where more than 300 people attended, in Buenos Aires, in Accra and in Shanghai at the Alibaba headquarters. The page names no founders and reports no claim to land or self-rule.
entries_new.anchor: No permanent site; events in several cities

entries_new.name: Cafe Cursor
entries_new.mechanism: Builds a recurring worldwide community through short events in rented cafes.
entries_new.story: Cafe Cursor is a series of popup cafe takeovers where users of Cursor, an AI coding tool, meet to write code together. It appears on the Network School dashboard, a list of startup societies. The page says the first popup opened in September 2025, starting in San Francisco and New York, and that a network of local ambassadors has hosted more than 600 events in over 250 cities in more than 80 countries. It is a company community and claims no territory or self-rule.
entries_new.anchor: No permanent site; first events in San Francisco and New York

entries_new.name: Frontier Tower
entries_new.mechanism: Gives each floor of one acquired building its own theme and lead.
entries_new.story: Frontier Tower is a 16-floor building at 995 Market Street in San Francisco, described by the Network School dashboard as a vertical village for frontier technology and a startup society inspired by Zuzalu. The building was acquired in 2025, opened in April 2025, and early members moved in during May. Each floor has its own theme and lead, such as AI, crypto, biotech or neurotech, and the nearby Superhero Hotel provides shared housing. The page reports no legal claim to self-rule.

entries_new.name: Akiya Collective
entries_new.mechanism: Acquires vacant houses and runs them as a shared community.
entries_new.story: Akiya Collective turns abandoned houses in rural Japan, called akiya, into residencies and community hubs. The Network School dashboard says it crowdfunded in 2022, explored more than 100 sites and acquired its first property in 2024, after becoming a nonprofit, in Komoro, Nagano. Five houses are in its care in Komoro, with five satellite properties, and its community space hosted 50 residents across 15 events in 2025. The page reports no claim to self-rule.

entries_new.name: Amagi Life
entries_new.mechanism: Gives residents equity in shared land in exchange for their contributions.
entries_new.story: Amagi Life is a project to build a network of regenerative villages, meant to restore the land, with long-term residents and shared land ownership. The Network School dashboard says it was founded in 2024 and that its first village, Hidden Valley, is on Koh Phangan, Thailand, where construction and planning began in 2025. Residents earn equity through what they contribute instead of what they pay. The team presented on tokens at Devconnect in November 2025. The page names no founders or member count.

entries_new.name: Proto-Town
entries_new.mechanism: Combines housing, workshops and test ground on private land, with a development agreement from local government.
entries_new.story: Proto-Town is a ranch and hardware incubator in Lockhart, Texas, founded in 2024, where startup founders live on site and build and test machines such as autonomous bulldozers, drones and robots. The Network School dashboard gives its size as 1,200 acres, while also saying the county approved a development agreement for a 538-acre innovation hub in August 2025. It reports a $20 million seed round in late 2025, and preliminary plans filed in March 2026 for a nuclear research reactor estimated at $23 million.

entries_new.name: Nomad (coliving villages)
entries_new.mechanism: Builds modular homes members can rent or buy, using a Honduran special zone for its second site.
entries_new.story: Nomad is a coliving company that sells or rents modular homes it calls NODE homes, listed on the Network School dashboard with the slogan of coliving villages from the future. The page says its first version operates in Raleigh and a second is under construction in Roatán at Próspera, the special economic zone in Honduras. Its timeline runs from a prototype in 2023 to a Roatán groundbreaking in 2026, and its 2023 events drew more than 100 people. No founders or member count are stated.
entries_new.anchor: Raleigh, with a second site at Próspera, Roatán

entries_new.name: Traditional Dream Factory
entries_new.mechanism: Uses a DAO and tokens to govern a former farm as a community.
entries_new.story: Traditional Dream Factory, or TDF, is a village in Portugal built on a former poultry farm acquired in 2021 and turned into a shared living campus focused on restoring the land. The Network School dashboard says it uses a DAO, a structure where token holders vote, along with $TDF tokens for governance, and combines agroforestry, rewilding and paid hospitality. The page says hospitality completion was under way in 2026. The page reports no claim to self-rule.

sources.t: Network School dashboard: Traditional Dream Factory

entries_new.name: Small Farm Cities Africa
entries_new.mechanism: Builds a new farming settlement with its own jobs and cheap housing.
entries_new.story: Small Farm Cities Africa is a social impact startup in Malawi that builds low-cost farming communities. The Network State Atlas says the model combines drip-irrigated greenhouses, poultry, fish farming and very cheap housing so working-class residents can own homes. It lists the project as active since 2020 with more than 100 residents. No town or founder is named on the page. The listing reports no claim to separate rule.

sources.t: Network State Atlas: Small Farm Cities Africa

entries_new.name: Porta Norte
entries_new.mechanism: Gathers interested people online first and plans to choose land later.
entries_new.story: Porta Norte is a plan for a new town in Europe integrated with nature. The Network State Atlas lists it as forming since 2022, with the location still to be determined and more than 1,000 people recorded as interested, a figure the page does not treat as membership. The Network State Dashboard list carries the same description. Neither source names founders or a site, so no town has been reported as built.

entries_new.name: Culdesac Tempe
entries_new.mechanism: Builds a new neighbourhood from scratch with no cars.
entries_new.story: Culdesac Tempe is a car-free neighbourhood in Tempe, Arizona, listed on the Network School dashboard as a startup society. The page calls it the first car-free neighbourhood built from scratch in the United States, on a 17-acre site beside a light rail station. Ryan Johnson and Jeff Berens founded the company in 2018; ground broke in November 2019 and first residents moved in during May 2023. As of 2025 it had over 350 residents and 21 local businesses. The page reports no legal claim to self-rule.

entries_new.name: Bitcoin Learning Center
entries_new.mechanism: Builds a local community around Bitcoin through teaching and events.
entries_new.story: The Bitcoin Learning Center is a self-funded hub in Chiang Mai, Thailand, opened in 2024 and listed on the Network School dashboard, which calls it Asia's most active physical Bitcoin hub. A full-time team of seven runs university programmes, technical workshops and festivals, including the 2025 Bitcoin Thailand Summit, and the page says it partners with local government on self custody, meaning people holding their own Bitcoin keys. It holds no special legal status on the page.

sources.t: Network School dashboard: Bitcoin Learning Center

entries_new.name: Courteen association
entries_new.stopped_by: Merged with the East India Company under Oliver Cromwell
entries_new.mechanism: Obtained a royal licence to trade in the east alongside a company that already held a monopoly.
entries_new.story: The Courteen association was an English trading company formed in 1635 to break the East India Company's monopoly on trade with India. King Charles gave Sir William Courteen a licence to trade in the east wherever the East India Company had no presence. It lost ships, collapsed in 1636, and was bought in 1643 from Courteen's widow by the merchant Maurice Thomson. It renamed itself the Assada company in 1649, and in 1657 a settlement ordered by Oliver Cromwell merged it with its rival.

entries_new.name: Royal Guipuzcoan Company of Caracas
entries_new.stopped_by: Merged into the Royal Company of the Philippines
entries_new.mechanism: Took a royal monopoly on one colony's trade and defended it with its own warships at its own expense.
entries_new.story: The Royal Guipuzcoan Company of Caracas was a Spanish chartered company, a business given special rights by a ruler, founded by wealthy Basques in 1728 to break the Dutch hold on cocoa in Venezuela. It alone could sell European goods in Caracas province and ship Venezuelan crops to Spain, and it kept its own warships and privateers. Its first ships in 1730 met a Creole refusal to sell cocoa and an uprising. After British captures of its ships it merged in 1785 into the Royal Company of the Philippines.

entries_new.name: Royal Company of the Philippines
entries_new.mechanism: Took a state monopoly on trade with a colony, with the colony's main port closed to foreign ships.
entries_new.story: The Royal Company of the Philippines was a Spanish chartered company set up by royal decree of Charles III on 10 March 1785, under Francisco Cabarrús, to monopolise trade between Spain and the Philippines. The decree closed Manila to foreign ships, and capital reached 10 million pesos by the end of 1785. Manila merchants and the British fought its monopoly, and it declined from 1794. It stopped working in 1829, after Spain lost its American territories, and was declared extinct by decree in 1834. A list on another page gives its end as 1814.

entries_new.name: Spanish Company
aka: President, Assistants and Fellowship of Merchants of England trading into Spain and Portugal
entries_new.laws: Own power to fine and imprison; own consuls to settle disputes abroad
entries_new.mechanism: Held a crown charter that gave its members exclusive trade, their own courts and consuls abroad, and the power to imprison.
entries_new.story: The Spanish Company was an English body of merchants given a monopoly on English trade with Spain and Portugal, under charters of 1530, 1577, 1604 and 1605. The 1605 charter named 557 founding members and let the company imprison or fine wrongdoers. It also forbade customs officers to accept goods bound for Spain or Portugal from anyone outside the fellowship, and let the company appoint its own consuls to settle disputes among members in those countries. The article gives no date for its end.
entries_new.anchor: England; trading to Spain and Portugal

entries_new.name: Eastland Company
aka: Company of Merchants of the East
entries_new.laws: Its own courts and laws under charter
entries_new.mechanism: Held a crown charter with its own governor, courts and laws for trade in one sea.
entries_new.story: The Eastland Company was an English crown-chartered company founded in 1579 to trade with Scandinavia and the Baltic and to challenge the Hanseatic League, a league of northern German trading towns. Its charter made it a body politic with its own seal, governor, courts and laws. Most Baltic trade stayed with Dutch rivals. Parliament's Trade Act 1672 opened trade with Sweden, Denmark and Norway to everyone, despite the charter, and let any Englishman join for 40 shillings. The article calls this a mortal blow.

entries_new.name: Barbary Company
entries_new.mechanism: Used a collective crown licence for exclusive trade with one foreign country.
entries_new.story: The Barbary Company, or Marocco Company, was created by a 1585 patent from Queen Elizabeth to the Earls of Warwick and Leicester and about 40 London merchants, giving them exclusive English trade with Morocco for 12 years. It swapped English cloth for Moroccan sugar. It was never incorporated, had no governor or court of assistants, and its name was only conventional. The charter expired in 1597. The article suggests the success of the Levant Company contributed to its commercial defeat.

entries_new.name: Venice Company
entries_new.founder: Thomas Cordell, William Garway and Edward Holmden
entries_new.mechanism: Held a time-limited crown monopoly over trade with one foreign state's colonies.
entries_new.story: The Venice Company was an English chartered company established in 1583 by Thomas Cordell, William Garway and Edward Holmden for an initial seven years. It held a monopoly on trade around the Venetian colonies in the Mediterranean, swapping English woollens for spices, currants and silk. When its charter and that of the Turkey Company both ran out in 1592, Queen Elizabeth approved one charter merging them into the Levant Company, which lasted until 1825.

entries_new.name: Swedish Levant Company
entries_new.mechanism: Held a limited monopoly from its own parliament, backed by a treaty with a foreign empire.
entries_new.story: The Swedish Levant Company was a Swedish chartered company founded on 20 February 1738, after a 1737 trade agreement with the Ottoman Empire, with the exclusive right to trade in the Levant, the eastern Mediterranean coast, for ten years. Its exports were tax-free, and only Swedish merchants could invest in its capital of 200,000 daler. The charter was renewed until 1748. Profits fell, a 1752 plan to revive trade failed, and the charter was revoked in 1756.

entries_new.name: Hollow Sword Blade Company
aka: Governor and Company for Making Hollow Sword Blades in England
entries_new.mechanism: Used the broad powers in an old sword-making charter to run a bank around another company's monopoly.
entries_new.story: The Hollow Sword Blades Company was founded in England in 1691 by the goldsmith Sir Stephen Evance to make swords, with works at Shotley Bridge in Durham. Its charter came on condition of a £50,000 loan to the government and let it buy land and issue stock without limit. In 1700 a syndicate bought it to run a bank, because the Bank of England held the legal monopoly on banking. It became a stepping stone to the South Sea Company.

entries_new.name: South Sea Company
entries_new.mechanism: Exchanged government debt for shares and a state-granted monopoly on the slave trade to Spanish America.
entries_new.story: The South Sea Company was a British joint-stock company founded in January 1711 to take over and cut the cost of the national debt. In 1713 it received the Asiento, a monopoly on supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America, and it transported over 34,000 people across the Atlantic. Its share price peaked in 1720 and collapsed, ruining thousands of investors in the South Sea Bubble. A parliamentary inquiry disgraced politicians and confiscated unlawful gains. The company was restructured and continued for more than a century.

entries_new.name: Barbados proprietors: Courteen and Carlisle
entries_new.founder: Sir William Courteen; Earl of Carlisle
entries_new.mechanism: Used a king's grant to make one man lord of an island and lease it to settlers.
entries_new.story: Barbados was fought over from 1627 to 1629 by two English men holding competing royal grants. Sir William Courteen paid for the first settlement. The Earl of Carlisle obtained a grant of Barbados and other Caribbee islands without his knowledge; the Earl of Pembroke won a reversal, and Carlisle won it back. In June 1628 Carlisle leased 10,000 acres to London merchants. Courteen's men seized Carlisle's governor in February 1629 and sent him to England in chains. King Charles sided with Carlisle, and Courteen's influence ended on 21 December 1629.

entries_new.name: Republic of Hout Bay
entries_new.founder: Hout Bay Lions and Rotary Club charities
entries_new.mechanism: Sold souvenir passports and a flag at mock border posts on public roads.
entries_new.story: The Republic of Hout Bay was a tourism stunt in a seaside town near Cape Town, South Africa. In 1987 the local Lions and Rotary Club charities set up checkpoints on the roads into town, where volunteers stopped drivers and walkers on weekends and holidays and sold them passports, with the money going to charity. Getaway magazine says some also saw it as resistance to apartheid, then in force. The checkpoints have ended, and shops still sell the passports as souvenirs.

sources.t: Have you been to The Republic of Hout Bay? (Getaway)

entries_new.name: Kingdom of Finismund
entries_new.founder: King Petrus Máximus I (title used on the wiki)
entries_new.mechanism: Declared claims on paper over unclaimed land and joined clubs of other micronations.
entries_new.story: The Kingdom of Finismund, formally Finis Mundi Terra, was a hobby micronation from Spain that claimed parts of Antarctica, around Marie Byrd Land and south of Queen Maud Land, plus Bir Tawil, the land between Egypt and Sudan. A micronation wiki, the only source found, says it was founded in November 2008 under a King Petrus Máximus and gives both 8 and 9 November. It ended on 1 December 2009 when another hobby state's email said the king had quit, and others divided the claims. No state recognised it.
entries_new.anchor: Spain (base of the founder); claims in Antarctica

entries_new.name: Federal Republic of Lostisland
entries_new.founder: Group of Russian students; Yaroslav Mar later head
entries_new.mechanism: Runs online as a direct democracy with symbolic paper claims to remote islands.
entries_new.story: Lostisland began as a Russian-language roleplaying game in July 2008, started by Russian students, and became a micronation in September 2010 and a federal republic in April 2013, according to a micronation wiki. It calls itself a cultural and social project, makes laws by referendum, and holds no land, with symbolic claims to Hunter Island in the South Pacific and Alexander Island in Antarctica. Yaroslav Mar is listed as President for Life and the population as 260 in December 2024. No UN member state recognises it.

entries_new.name: Kingdom of St. Charlie
entries_new.mechanism: Declared a family house and garden a kingdom, without seceding in practice.
entries_new.story: The Kingdom of St. Charlie was a hobby micronation consisting of one house and garden near Rome, Italy, on a property bought in 1982. A micronation wiki says the Italian architect Patrizio Ruvolo declared himself King Patrizio on 25 December 2000 as a Christmas joke, with a census population of five and no currency. He abdicated on 15 November 2008, citing health and money problems, and a Federal Republic of St. Charlie replaced it a week later. The wiki reports no recognition by any government.

entries_new.name: Kingdom of TorHavn
entries_new.mechanism: Publishes its own law code and citizenship online while holding no land.
entries_new.story: The Kingdom of TorHavn is an online micronation that calls itself a model country project, known from its own website with copyright dates from 1999 to 2007. The site describes a dual monarchy under what it calls Enlightened Absolutism, a written King's Code of laws, and citizens who swear an oath of loyalty. It says it is landless, has not yet acquired land, lacks full diplomatic relations with any state, and has no functioning economy. The page does not name a founder or a founding year.

entries_new.name: Foreign concessions in Tianjin
entries_new.recognition: China, by treaty, and the concession powers
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign states took city districts by treaty after defeating China and ran them under their own law.
entries_new.story: The foreign concessions in Tianjin were districts of a Chinese port city ceded by the Qing dynasty to outside powers. The first were granted to Britain and France in 1860 after military defeats of China. Japan, Germany, Russia, Austria-Hungary, Italy and Belgium joined between 1895 and 1900, each with its own prisons, schools, barracks and hospitals, and nine existed before the Second World War. The European settlements covered 13 square kilometres. Britain gave up its rights in 1943, and by 1947 all had returned to China.

entries_new.name: American concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Ran a district informally under another power's oversight, without a grant.
entries_new.story: The American concession in Tianjin, China, was never formally requested or granted. A de facto American area was run from 1869 to 1880, mainly under the British mission, and in 1902 this informal territory became part of the British concession. The United States kept a garrison at Tianjin afterward, from the 15th Infantry from 1912 to 1938 and then the Marine Corps until 8 December 1941, when the United States entered the Second World War.

entries_new.name: Austro-Hungarian concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Held a reward district under its own law, a council and a small garrison.
entries_new.story: Austria-Hungary gained a concession of 150 acres in Tianjin, China, as its reward for joining the alliance that suppressed the Boxer Rebellion. About 30,000 people lived there, kept in order by 40 marines and 80 Chinese militia. A town council led by the consul and the military commander ran it under Austro-Hungarian law, with its own school, prison and hospital. China occupied it when it declared war in 1917 and ended the lease on 14 August. Austria gave up its claim in 1919 and Hungary in 1920.

entries_new.name: Belgian concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Claimed a district during peace talks, while the real money came from a tram and power monopoly.
entries_new.story: The Belgian concession in Tianjin, China, was established in 1902 after the envoy Maurice Joostens claimed a parcel in talks following the defeat of the Boxer rebels. It lay on the eastern bank of the Hai River, and neither the government nor Belgian business invested in it, so it stayed nominal. An agreement to return it was signed in August 1929 and approved by the Belgian parliament in 1931. A Belgian company kept a 50-year monopoly on Tianjin's trams and electric lighting until Japan's army took it over in 1943.

entries_new.name: British concession in Tianjin
entries_new.challenge: Japanese blockade of 1939 and occupation of 1941
entries_new.mechanism: A lease in perpetuity from China to a foreign crown, sublet to private owners and run by a council.
entries_new.story: The British concession in Tianjin, China, held the city's trade and financial centres on about 200 acres on the right bank of the Hai River. It was held on a lease in perpetuity from the Chinese government to the British Crown, which sublet plots to private owners. A municipal council ran it from Gordon Hall on Victoria Road. Japan blockaded it in the Tientsin incident of June 1939 and occupied it from December 1941. Britain was the first of the powers to give up its concessions, in 1943.

entries_new.name: French concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Held a district by concession with its own municipal council and consul.
entries_new.story: The French concession in Tianjin, China, was established in 1860 and lasted until 1946. Its buildings included the French Consulate, the Municipal Council, the French Club and a Catholic cathedral, and many survive. Its financial street was the Rue de France, now Jiefang Lu. The diplomat and writer Paul Claudel served as consul from 1906 to 1909, and the scientist Father Emile Licent worked there from 1914 to 1939 and founded a museum of natural history.

entries_new.name: German concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Used a naval presence and a treaty to hold a trading district.
entries_new.story: The German concession in Tianjin, China, covered about 2 square kilometres south of the Hai River between the British and Japanese areas. German merchants had asked for protection in 1877, and a further concession followed after Germany leased Kiautschou Bay in 1898. Trading houses and a German-Asian bank set up there. China occupied it after declaring war on the Central Powers in August 1917, and in 1919 it became the First Special District under permanent Chinese administration.

entries_new.name: Italian concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Held a district under a consul, backed by a garrison and naval vessels.
entries_new.story: The Italian concession in Tianjin, China, was granted on 7 September 1901 and taken over on 7 June 1902, under an Italian consul. In 1935 it had about 6,261 people, including about 536 foreigners, and in the Second World War a garrison of about 600 troops. Japan occupied it on 10 September 1943, when Italy signed an armistice. The Italian Social Republic then ceded it to Wang Jingwei's Japanese-sponsored Chinese government, and Italy's surrender of its rights in the 1947 peace treaty was a formality.

entries_new.name: Japanese concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Gained a district after a war and enlarged it after another.
entries_new.story: The Japanese concession in Tianjin, China, was set up in 1898 after the First Sino-Japanese War and enlarged from 1900 to 1902 after the Boxer Rebellion. Puyi, the last Qing emperor, lived in Tianjin from 1924 to 1931, when the Japanese army took him to Dalian. In 1937 Japan's army occupied the rest of the city except the foreign concessions, which it took in 1941 and 1943. The Japanese concession ceased to exist with Japan's surrender in 1945.

entries_new.name: Russian concession in Tianjin
entries_new.mechanism: Marked out land by right of conquest first and had it confirmed by treaty after.
entries_new.story: A treaty of 31 December 1900 granted Russia a concession in Tianjin, China, though its general had already claimed the area by right of conquest and begun placing boundary markers. At 398 hectares on the left bank of the Peiho River, in two separate districts, it was the largest of the foreign concessions. Russian trade there was small and the land stayed largely undeveloped. China's Beiyang government took it back in 1920, and the Soviet Union renounced its claim in 1924.

entries_new.name: International Authority for the Ruhr
entries_new.stopped_by: Replaced by the European Coal and Steel Community
entries_new.recognition: United States, United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg, West Germany
entries_new.mechanism: Six states used a treaty to put a region's coal and steel exports under a joint council.
entries_new.story: The International Authority for the Ruhr was a body set up by the Western Allies to control coal and steel from the Ruhr area of West Germany, with its seat in Düsseldorf. It came from the London Six-Power Conference of 1948, and its statute took effect on 28 April 1949. France, the United States and Britain had three votes each, the Benelux countries one each, and Germany three. Its main power was fixing how much coal Germany exported. The Treaty of Paris of 1951 replaced it with the European Coal and Steel Community, and its functions ended on 25 June 1952.

entries_new.name: B330
entries_new.stopped_by: Bigelow laid off all staff in March 2020
entries_new.cost: US$25 million for a 60-day lease of one third (2014 quote)
entries_new.mechanism: A private company planned to own a station in orbit and lease space on it to countries and companies.
entries_new.story: The B330, earlier called the Nautilus and BA 330, was an inflatable space habitat developed privately by Bigelow Aerospace from 2010, with 330 cubic metres of room for up to six people. In 2014 the company quoted US$25 million to lease a third of it for 60 days. It signed launch agreements with United Launch Alliance in 2016 and 2017. Test articles were built on the ground, and none flew. Bigelow stopped all work in March 2020 when it laid off its 88 staff.
entries_new.anchor: Built in North Las Vegas; planned for low Earth orbit

entries_new.name: Sundancer
entries_new.cost: US$7.9 million estimated for a one-week trip (2005)
entries_new.mechanism: A private prototype intended to become the first piece of a company-owned station.
entries_new.story: Sundancer was a planned prototype space habitat from Bigelow Aerospace, and would have been its first expandable module rated to carry people. It was under construction in North Las Vegas, with a launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 reported for 2010, then slipping to 2011 and 2014. In July 2011 the company dropped it so the larger B330 would come first. It was meant to be the starting point of a commercial space complex, with a one-week trip estimated in 2005 at US$7.9 million.

entries_new.name: Galaxy (Bigelow module)
entries_new.mechanism: A private test craft on the way to a company-owned station.
entries_new.story: Galaxy, earlier called Guardian, was a cancelled prototype space habitat from Bigelow Aerospace, meant to be the third craft the company launched on the way to a commercial space station. It was to test improved electronics and life support, with 16.7 cubic metres inside. In August 2007 the company said launch costs had tripled and the Genesis flights had gone well, so it would not launch. Its systems, and possibly the whole craft, would be tested on the ground instead.

entries_new.name: Genesis I
entries_new.mechanism: A private company put its own uncrewed habitat in orbit to prove the design for later stations.
entries_new.story: The first Genesis module was an experimental inflatable space habitat built privately by Bigelow Aerospace and launched on 12 July 2006 on a Dnepr rocket from Dombarovsky in Russia. It was a one-third scale model of the planned full-size module, expanding in orbit to 11.5 cubic metres inside over about ten minutes. Designed to work for six months, its electronics ran for over two and a half years. It carried no people. It completed its 10,000th orbit on 8 May 2008.
entries_new.anchor: Low Earth orbit; launched from Dombarovsky, Russia

entries_new.name: Genesis II
entries_new.mechanism: A private company put its own uncrewed habitat in orbit to test systems for later stations.
entries_new.story: Genesis II was the second experimental inflatable space habitat built by Bigelow Aerospace, launched in 2007 from Dombarovsky in Russia after nearly a year of US export control and other regulatory steps. It matched the first Genesis module in size and carried 22 cameras. Its electronics stopped after two and a half years, leaving it a derelict spacecraft. A US Air Force alert in 2019 gave it a 5.6 percent chance of hitting the Soviet satellite Kosmos 1300. It re-entered the atmosphere on 2 September 2025.
entries_new.anchor: Low Earth orbit; launched from Dombarovsky, Russia

entries_new.name: Bigelow Commercial Space Station
entries_new.mechanism: A private company planned to own and rent out an orbital complex.
entries_new.story: The Bigelow Commercial Space Station was a private orbital station planned by Bigelow Aerospace. A 2005 version, CSS Skywalker, was pitched as a first space hotel with a projected room rate of US$1 million per night and a first module launch in 2010. A 2010 plan, later named Space Complex Alpha, was reduced by January 2013 to two B330 modules, the first no earlier than 2016. None of it flew, and the company laid off its staff in March 2020.

entries_new.name: Urbit
entries_new.pop: A few thousand active users (The Point, 2022); 10,000+ planet owners (directory figure)
entries_new.mechanism: Gives each user a numbered identity recorded on a blockchain and run on a private server.
entries_new.story: Urbit is a personal server platform, a private computer in a peer-to-peer network, created by Curtis Yarvin, whom Wikipedia describes as a far-right blogger. The network launched in 2013. Each user's identity is a numbered address recorded on the Ethereum blockchain. Tlon, the company Yarvin founded to build it, took funding from Peter Thiel's Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz. Critics called the design digital feudalism in 2010, and the Urbit Foundation's director denied it in 2022. The Network State Atlas lists more than 10,000 owners of the address type called planets; The Point estimated a few thousand active users in 2022.

entries_new.name: Mars Base Camp
entries_new.mechanism: A company design for a crewed outpost in Mars orbit, dependent on NASA adopting it.
entries_new.story: Mars Base Camp is a concept from Lockheed Martin for a crewed laboratory orbiting Mars, proposed to NASA and detailed at a conference in March 2017. Space.com reported a station with six people on a year of occupation that could be circling Mars by 2028, with a reusable craft making two-week trips to the surface. As of April 2018 NASA had not formally proposed the mission in a federal budget.

entries_new.name: Whaleship Sharon mutiny
entries_new.mechanism: Crew members killed the captain at sea.
entries_new.story: The Sharon was a whaleship from Fairhaven, Massachusetts, that went through mass desertions and mutinies. Wikipedia's list of mutinies says its captain, described there as cruel, was murdered and dismembered by four Polynesians who had been pressed into service on board. The row gives no date and places the case in the list's 19th century section, beside entries from 1857. It names no later outcome for the killers or the ship.

entries_new.name: Whaleship Junior mutiny
entries_new.mechanism: Crew members killed the officers to take the ship.
entries_new.story: The Junior was a whaleship on which Cyrus Plummer and several others staged a mutiny in 1857, murdering Captain Archibald Mellen and Third Mate John Smith. The mutineers were captured and found guilty in the autumn of 1858. Plummer was sentenced to hang and his accomplices received life sentences. The case made national and international news. President James Buchanan granted Plummer a stay of execution, and President Ulysses S. Grant eventually pardoned him.
